how_it_works: Caption:Five steps, in order. Only the deterministic checks decide an outcome.
Markdown:

Markdown:
  1. The evaluation is run. ATLAS runs the project's own evaluation in an isolated container and records what happened: which rows each step learned from, which rows were tested, and the predictions.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §4.3, §10
  2. Deterministic checks decide. Fixed checks read that record and decide whether the evaluation breaks a rule of the claim, for example the same person on both sides of the split. No AI model takes part in this decision.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §5, §6; README.md, Roles
  3. The AI may propose a revision, which ATLAS does not trust. An AI model (Nemotron) may read the project and propose a revised evaluation script. The proposal is only checked for allowed changes, and the model's text is never evidence.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §9 items 1-3, §11; README.md, Roles
  4. A human approves by typing the code hash. A person approves the original code and each exact revision by typing the start of its code hash; the approval is bound to the snapshot and code hashes. Any change to the code needs a new approval.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §9 item 5; README.md, Safety controls and their reviews, and Setup and running
  5. The revision runs sealed and is re-checked. The approved revision runs sealed in the isolated container, and the same checks judge it again. The model never declares success.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §9 item 6, §6

Markdown:
  • Isolated Docker runner: no network, a non-root user and a read-only filesystem, with limits on memory, CPU, processes and time. If the container runner is unavailable, ATLAS stops and never runs code directly on the host computer.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §10; README.md, Safety and honesty rules
  • Typed approval bound to the snapshot and code hashes: an approval names the exact original or revision code, and the runner refuses to run any other code.
    Source: docs/SPEC.md §9 item 5; README.md, Safety controls and their reviews, and Setup and running
  • The AI's text is never evidence: its diffs, explanations and raw replies are labelled untrusted, and outcomes come only from the trusted evaluator.
    Source: README.md, Safety and honesty rules and Roles
  • Spending is reserved before every request, with caps: per run locally, and per session, per day and per route on the hosted demo. Totals are estimates, not billing.
    Source: README.md, How ATLAS uses NVIDIA Nemotron (Cost accounting); docs/HOSTED_OPERATIONS.md §1, §4
  • The hosted demo executes no project or candidate code: it replays recorded runs, and in a hosted live session it checks the AI's proposals and shows them as not executed here.
    Source: README.md, Architecture; docs/HOSTED_OPERATIONS.md §1; docs/SPEC.md §13
  • Recorded runs are re-verified before display: every recorded hash is recomputed from the files, and a changed file shows "evidence changed" instead of a result. This detects changes since recording; it does not authenticate a run whose files and recorded hashes were both rewritten.
    Source: docs/HOSTED_OPERATIONS.md §1; README.md, Architecture
Caption:The README's limitations, in plain words; none is softened. Expert view shows the original wording.

Markdown:
  • ATLAS can trace which rows each step learned from only for the supported steps. Its recorder runs inside the project's own process and is not tamper-proof; its fingerprints do not prove that every kind of preprocessing was observed; and a missing trace does not prove that a step did not happen.
    Fit provenance covers only the bounded supported path. The in-process recorder is not tamper-proof, fingerprints don't prove arbitrary preprocessing was observed, and missing traces don't prove absence.
  • Tracing starts at the feature table the project supplies. How those features were extracted or normalised before that is not checked.
    Provenance begins at the supplied feature table; upstream feature extraction and normalization are not verified.
  • ATLAS cannot detect a dependence between rows (for example, the same person) that the project did not declare. Some declared dependences have no rule in this version and are reported as not assessed.
    Policy cannot detect dependence the user did not declare. Some declared dependence has no supported rule in V1 and stays NOT_ASSESSED.
  • Without IDs for the original observations, duplicate detection only compares exact values, and it can leave possible duplicates unresolved.
    Duplicate detection without source-observation identity is an exact-value screen and can leave unresolved candidates.
  • The time-based checks verify only the availability and separation rules the project declares, and the window check verifies only the declared recording streams and window intervals. None of them proves that training and test data are statistically independent.
    Temporal assertions verify declared availability and separation rules, and split.no_window_overlap verifies declared stream identity and window intervals. None of them is proof of statistical independence.
  • A green result means only that the listed checks passed, within the coverage stated.
    A green outcome means only that the listed assertions passed within the stated coverage.
  • There are no held-out test projects: they were cut for the submission, so every detection result here is on the development projects ATLAS was built on.
    Held-out cases (T-10) were cut for the submission; every detection result here is on development cases (DECISIONS.md "T-11 re-scope and T-10 (lead, 2026-10-19)").
